questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When salts of alkali metals are introduced into a non-luminous Bunsen flame, characteristic atomic emission lines are observed. Potassium chloride imparts a characteristic lilac flame dominated by an emission line at $\lambda_{\text{K}} = 766.5\text{ nm}$, whereas sodium chloride imparts an intense golden-yellow flame dominated by an emission line at $\lambda_{\text{Na}} = 589.2\text{ nm}$. Taking Planck's constant as $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$, the speed of light as $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, and Avogadro's constant as $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, calculate the ratio of the individual photon energy of the sodium emission to that of the potassium emission ($E_{\text{Na}} / E_{\text{K}}$), and determine the molar excitation energy (in $\text{kJ/mol}$) corresponding to the sodium emission line.
options: A) $1.301$ and $203.1\text{ kJ/mol}$
B) $0.769$ and $203.1\text{ kJ/mol}$
C) $1.301$ and $156.1\text{ kJ/mol}$
D) $0.769$ and $156.1\text{ kJ/mol}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: The photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength according to the Planck-Einstein relation: $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$. Therefore, the ratio of photon energies is given by the inverse ratio of their emission wavelengths: $\frac{E_{\text{Na}}}{E_{\text{K}}} = \frac{\lambda_{\text{K}}}{\lambda_{\text{Na}}} = \frac{766.5\text{ nm}}{589.2\text{ nm}} \approx 1.301$. An inverted value of $0.769$ corresponds to the erroneous direct ratio $\lambda_{\text{Na}} / \lambda_{\text{K}}$. Step 2: The molar excitation energy for sodium emission is obtained by multiplying the single photon energy by Avogadro's number: $E_{\text{molar}}(\text{Na}) = \frac{N_A hc}{\lambda_{\text{Na}}} = \frac{(6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1})(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s})(3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m/s})}{589.2 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}} = \frac{1.197 \times 10^{-1} \times 10^6}{589.2}\text{ J/mol} \approx 203.1\text{ kJ/mol}$. Hence, calculating the molar energy using potassium's wavelength yields $156.1\text{ kJ/mol}$, representing an erroneous assignment. Applying both correct formulas yields $1.301$ and $203.1\text{ kJ/mol}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
In flame photometry, thermal excitation of valence electrons in alkaline earth and alkali metal chlorides yields characteristic emission spectra when the electronic excitation energy matches the visible spectrum. Consider the following assertions:
(1) $\text{BeCl}_2$ produces a persistent green coloration in a Bunsen flame.
(2) $\text{MgCl}_2$ produces an intense violet flame.
(3) $\text{CaCl}_2$ imparts a brick-red coloration ($\lambda \approx 622\text{ nm}$) to the flame.
(4) $\text{SrCl}_2$ imparts a crimson-red coloration ($\lambda \approx 671\text{ nm}$) to the flame.
(5) $\text{BaCl}_2$ imparts an apple-green coloration ($\lambda \approx 554\text{ nm}$) to the flame.
(6) $\text{CsCl}$ imparts a distinctive blue coloration ($\lambda \approx 455\text{ nm}$) to the flame.
(7) The absence of flame coloration for beryllium and magnesium is attributed to their exceptionally high ionization enthalpies and small atomic radii, which prevent thermal excitation by the burner flame.
Determine the total number of assertions that are scientifically TRUE.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Inspect assertions (1) and (2): Beryllium and magnesium atoms have extremely small atomic sizes and correspondingly very high ionization enthalpies ($899\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $737\text{ kJ/mol}$ respectively). The thermal energy supplied by a standard Bunsen flame ($\,\sim 1800\text{--}2000^\circ\text{C}$) is insufficient to excite their valence electrons to higher energy levels; hence, neither $\text{Be}$ nor $\text{Mg}$ imparts any color to the flame. Statements (1) and (2) are therefore FALSE. Step 2: For calcium, strontium, and barium, larger atomic sizes and lower ionization enthalpies allow thermal excitation, and electronic relaxation emits in the visible spectrum: $\text{Ca}$ emits brick-red (Statement 3 is TRUE), $\text{Sr}$ emits crimson-red (Statement 4 is TRUE), and $\text{Ba}$ emits apple-green (Statement 5 is TRUE). Step 3: For cesium, the lowest ionization enthalpy among stable alkali metals enables excitation with emission in the blue region ($\,\sim 455\text{ nm}$), hence Statement 6 is TRUE. Step 4: Statement 7 correctly explains the absence of flame test for $\text{Be}$ and $\text{Mg}$ based on high ionization energy, and is TRUE. Thus, statements (3), (4), (5), (6), and (7) are TRUE, giving a total of exactly 5 true assertions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates follows the endothermic dissociation equilibrium: $\text{MCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{MO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$, where decomposition becomes spontaneous under standard atmospheric pressure ($P_{\text{CO}_2} = 1.0\text{ bar}$) when the standard Gibbs energy change $\Delta G^\circ = 0$. Given the thermodynamic parameters: for $\text{MgCO}_3$, $\Delta H^\circ = +117.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +175.0\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$; for $\text{SrCO}_3$, $\Delta H^\circ = +234.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +171.0\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$. Assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ remain constant over the temperature range, determine the minimum decomposition temperatures $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{MgCO}_3)$ and $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{SrCO}_3)$ (rounded to the nearest integer Kelvin), and identify the fundamental structural cause responsible for the greater thermal stability of $\text{SrCO}_3$.
options: A) $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{MgCO}_3) \approx 669\text{ K}$, $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{SrCO}_3) \approx 1368\text{ K}$; lower polarizing power of $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ minimizes distortion of the carbonate anion
B) $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{MgCO}_3) \approx 1368\text{ K}$, $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{SrCO}_3) \approx 669\text{ K}$; higher lattice energy of $\text{MgCO}_3$ provides superior thermodynamic stability
C) $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{MgCO}_3) \approx 845\text{ K}$, $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{SrCO}_3) \approx 1120\text{ K}$; higher hydration energy of strontium stabilizes the solid salt
D) $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{MgCO}_3) \approx 669\text{ K}$, $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{SrCO}_3) \approx 1368\text{ K}$; larger charge density of $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ strengthens the $\text{Sr-C}$ covalent bond
questions.explanation: Step 1: Spontaneous thermal decomposition under $P_{\text{CO}_2} = 1.0\text{ bar}$ requires $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T_{\text{dec}}\Delta S^\circ = 0$, yielding $T_{\text{dec}} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ}$. Step 2: Substituting thermodynamic parameters for $\text{MgCO}_3$: $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{MgCO}_3) = \frac{117.0 \times 10^3\text{ J/mol}}{175.0\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}} \approx 668.6\text{ K} \approx 669\text{ K}$. Step 3: Substituting parameters for $\text{SrCO}_3$: $T_{\text{dec}}(\text{SrCO}_3) = \frac{234.0 \times 10^3\text{ J/mol}}{171.0\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}} \approx 1368.4\text{ K} \approx 1368\text{ K}$. Step 4: Thermal stability of carbonates increases down Group 2 because polarizing power $\Phi = z/r$ decreases as cation radius increases ($\text{Mg}^{2+}: 72\text{ pm} < \text{Sr}^{2+}: 118\text{ pm}$). The smaller $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ cation exerts high polarization on the electron cloud of the carbonate anion ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}$), weakening a $\text{C-O}$ bond and facilitating decomposition into $\text{CO}_2$ and oxide. In addition, the lattice energy gained by forming $\text{MgO}$ is exceptionally large compared to $\text{SrO}$. Thus, lower polarizing power of $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ stabilizes $\text{SrCO}_3$, making option A correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The standard enthalpy of solution for an ionic salt is governed by the Born-Haber balance: $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{sol}} = \Delta H^\circ_{\text{lattice}} + \Delta H^\circ_{\text{hyd}}$, where $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{lattice}} > 0$ represents the endothermic dissociation into gaseous ions and $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{hyd}} < 0$ represents exothermic hydration. Down Group 2 from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, the aqueous solubility of hydroxides increases ($\text{Mg(OH)}_2 < \text{Ca(OH)}_2 < \text{Sr(OH)}_2 < \text{Ba(OH)}_2$), whereas the solubility of sulfates decreases ($\text{MgSO}_4 > \text{CaSO}_4 > \text{SrSO}_4 > \text{BaSO}_4$). Which of the following thermodynamic deductions rigorously explains this contrasting behavior?
options: A) For hydroxides, the small $\text{OH}^-$ radius makes lattice enthalpy decrease more rapidly down the group than hydration enthalpy; for sulfates, the large $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ radius keeps lattice enthalpy nearly constant while cation hydration enthalpy drops sharply
B) For hydroxides, hydration enthalpy increases down the group while lattice enthalpy remains constant; for sulfates, lattice enthalpy increases sharply due to the multivalent nature of sulfate
C) For both hydroxides and sulfates, hydration enthalpy remains invariant, and the solubility trends are dictated entirely by entropy of mixing
D) For hydroxides, the large $\text{OH}^-$ ion shields cation charge, making dissolution endothermic for barium; for sulfates, small $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ size makes barium sulfate highly covalent
questions.explanation: Step 1: According to Kapustinskii's equation, lattice energy scales as $U_{\text{lat}} \propto \frac{1}{r_+ + r_-}$, while individual cation hydration enthalpy scales as $|\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}^circ(\text{M}^{2+})| \propto \frac{1}{r_+}$. Step 2: For hydroxides, the anion $\text{OH}^-$ is relatively small ($r_- \approx 137\text{ pm}$). As $r_+$ increases from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ($72\text{ pm}$) to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ($135\text{ pm}$), the internuclear sum $(r_+ + r_-)$ increases significantly (from $209\text{ pm}$ to $272\text{ pm}$), causing the lattice enthalpy to decrease by a large magnitude that outweighs the decrease in hydration enthalpy. Therefore, $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{sol}}$ becomes more exothermic/less endothermic, yielding increased solubility down the group. Step 3: For sulfates, the $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ anion is bulky ($r_- \approx 230\text{ pm}$). The internuclear distance $(r_+ + r_-)$ changes only modestly from $302\text{ pm}$ to $365\text{ pm}$, so the lattice energy decreases very little. However, $|\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}^circ(\text{M}^{2+})|$ decreases drastically with increasing cation size. Hence, the loss of hydration energy dominates over lattice energy reduction, causing $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{sol}}$ to become increasingly endothermic, which sharply reduces solubility down the group. Option A correctly captures this foundational principle.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Lithium exhibits an anomalous diagonal relationship with magnesium, including their reactions with atmospheric nitrogen to form ionic nitrides and the thermal instability of their carbonates. An equimolar dry solid mixture containing exactly $1.00\text{ mol}$ of pure lithium nitride ($\text{Li}_3\text{N}$) and $1.00\text{ mol}$ of pure magnesium nitride ($\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2$) is completely hydrolyzed in excess hot water. The gaseous ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) evolved is collected quantitatively and neutralized completely by titration against $1.00\text{ M}$ standard aqueous hydrochloric acid ($\text{HCl}$). What is the total volume (in liters, rounded to the nearest integer) of $1.00\text{ M}\ \text{HCl}$ consumed in this neutralization?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Write the balanced stoichiometric equation for the hydrolysis of lithium nitride: $\text{Li}_3\text{N}(s) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 3\text{LiOH}(aq) + \text{NH}_3(g)$. Hydrolysis of $1.00\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Li}_3\text{N}$ produces exactly $1.00\text{ mol}$ of gaseous ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$). Step 2: Write the balanced stoichiometric equation for the hydrolysis of magnesium nitride: $\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2(s) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 3\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + 2\text{NH}_3(g)$. Hydrolysis of $1.00\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2$ produces exactly $2.00\text{ moles}$ of $\text{NH}_3(g)$. Step 3: Total moles of ammonia evolved: $n(\text{NH}_3) = 1.00 + 2.00 = 3.00\text{ moles}$. Step 4: Ammonia neutralizes hydrochloric acid in a $1:1$ molar stoichiometry: $\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{HCl}(aq) \to \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(aq)$. Hence, $n(\text{HCl}) = n(\text{NH}_3) = 3.00\text{ moles}$. Applying the molarity relation: $V = \frac{n}{M} = \frac{3.00\text{ mol}}{1.00\text{ mol/L}} = 3.00\text{ L}$. The integer answer is therefore 3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: An aqueous test solution contains $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ cations, each at an initial concentration of $1.00 \times 10^{-2}\text{ M}$. At $298\text{ K}$, the solubility product constants of barium sulfate and strontium sulfate are $K_{sp}(\text{BaSO}_4) = 1.10 \times 10^{-10}$ and $K_{sp}(\text{SrSO}_4) = 3.20 \times 10^{-7}$, respectively. Solid sodium sulfate is added gradually with negligible change in volume. Determine the sulfate ion concentration $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$ at which $\text{BaSO}_4$ begins to precipitate, and calculate the percentage of initial $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ remaining unprecipitated in solution at the exact instant $\text{SrSO}_4$ just begins to precipitate.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Precipitation of $\text{BaSO}_4$ commences when the ionic product equals $K_{sp}(\text{BaSO}_4)$: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = K_{sp}(\text{BaSO}_4) \implies [\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = \frac{1.10 \times 10^{-10}}{1.00 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.10 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$. Step 2: Precipitation of $\text{SrSO}_4$ commences when $[\text{Sr}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = K_{sp}(\text{SrSO}_4) \implies [\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = \frac{3.20 \times 10^{-7}}{1.00 \times 10^{-2}} = 3.20 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M}$. Step 3: At this sulfate concentration, the residual concentration of dissolved $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ in equilibrium with solid $\text{BaSO}_4$ is: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]_{\text{rem}} = \frac{K_{sp}(\text{BaSO}_4)}{[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]} = \frac{1.10 \times 10^{-10}}{3.20 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 3.438 \times 10^{-6}\text{ M}$. Step 4: Calculating the percentage of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ remaining in solution: $\%\,\text{remaining} = \frac{[\text{Ba}^{2+}]_{\text{rem}}}{[\text{Ba}^{2+}]_0} \times 100\% = \frac{3.438 \times 10^{-6}\text{ M}}{1.00 \times 10^{-2}\text{ M}} \times 100\% \approx 0.03438\% \approx 0.034\%$. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Beryllium and aluminum share a pronounced diagonal relationship due to their virtually identical ionic charge-to-radius ratios ($\sim 64\text{ nm}^{-1}$ and $\sim 60\text{ nm}^{-1}$), causing both to dissolve in caustic alkali solutions with liberation of dihydrogen gas to form beryllate and aluminate complex ions. A $0.200\text{ mol}$ solid mixture containing only pure powdered beryllium and aluminum metals is treated with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide, yielding exactly $5.824\text{ L}$ of dry $\text{H}_2(g)$ measured at STP ($0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1.00\text{ atm}$, where the molar volume of an ideal gas is $22.4\text{ L/mol}$). What are the molar percentages of beryllium and aluminum in the original metal mixture?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Write the stoichiometric reactions for the dissolution of beryllium and aluminum in aqueous sodium hydroxide: For beryllium: $\text{Be}(s) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to \text{Na}_2[\text{Be(OH)}_4](aq) + \text{H}_2(g)$, showing $1\text{ mol}\ \text{Be} \to 1\text{ mol}\ \text{H}_2$. For aluminum: $2\text{Al}(s) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 2\text{Na}[\text{Al(OH)}_4](aq) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$, showing $1\text{ mol}\ \text{Al} \to 1.5\text{ mol}\ \text{H}_2$. Step 2: Total moles of dihydrogen gas evolved: $n(\text{H}_2) = \frac{5.824\text{ L}}{22.4\text{ L/mol}} = 0.260\text{ mol}$. Step 3: Let $n_{\text{Be}} = x$ and $n_{\text{Al}} = y$. Then $x + y = 0.200\text{ mol}$ and $x + 1.5y = 0.260\text{ mol}$. Subtracting the two equations yields: $0.5y = 0.060\text{ mol} \implies y = 0.120\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Al}$. Hence, $x = 0.200 - 0.120 = 0.080\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Be}$. Step 4: Calculating molar percentages: $\%\,\text{Be} = \frac{0.080}{0.200} \times 100\% = 40.0\%$, and $\%\,\text{Al} = \frac{0.120}{0.200} \times 100\% = 60.0\%$. Thus, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The thermal decomposition of solid sodium hydrogen carbonate proceeds according to the heterogeneous equilibrium: $2\text{NaHCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$. When an excess of pure $\text{NaHCO}_3(s)$ is sealed in an evacuated rigid $10.0\text{ L}$ reaction vessel at $373\text{ K}$, thermal equilibrium is established at a total pressure of $0.540\text{ bar}$. Given $R = 0.08314\text{ L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}$ and the molar mass of $\text{NaHCO}_3 = 84.0\text{ g/mol}$, calculate the equilibrium constant $K_p$ (in $\text{bar}^2$) at $373\text{ K}$, and determine the minimum initial mass of $\text{NaHCO}_3$ (in grams, rounded to one decimal place) required to establish this equilibrium inside the vessel.
options: A) $K_p = 0.0729\text{ bar}^2$ and $14.6\text{ g}$
B) $K_p = 0.2916\text{ bar}^2$ and $14.6\text{ g}$
C) $K_p = 0.0729\text{ bar}^2$ and $29.2\text{ g}$
D) $K_p = 0.5400\text{ bar}^2$ and $7.3\text{ g}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: In an initially evacuated vessel, $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ vapor are formed in an equimolar $1:1$ stoichiometric ratio. Therefore, the partial pressures are equal: $P_{\text{CO}_2} = P_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = \frac{P_{\text{total}}}{2} = \frac{0.540\text{ bar}}{2} = 0.270\text{ bar}$. Step 2: The equilibrium constant is: $K_p = P_{\text{CO}_2} \cdot P_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = (0.270)(0.270) = 0.0729\text{ bar}^2$. Forgetting to divide total pressure by 2 yields $(0.540)^2 = 0.2916\text{ bar}^2$. Step 3: Using the ideal gas equation, the total moles of gas present in the $10.0\text{ L}$ container at $373\text{ K}$ is: $n_{\text{gas}} = \frac{P_{\text{total}} V}{RT} = \frac{(0.540\text{ bar})(10.0\text{ L})}{(0.08314\text{ L}\cdot\text{bar}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\cdot\text{K}^{-1})(373\text{ K})} = \frac{5.40}{31.011} \approx 0.1741\text{ mol}$. Step 4: The chemical equation shows that decomposition of $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{NaHCO}_3$ generates $2\text{ mol}$ of total gas ($1\text{ mol}\ \text{CO}_2 + 1\text{ mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}$). Therefore, the moles of $\text{NaHCO}_3$ that must decompose is exactly equal to $n_{\text{gas}} = 0.1741\text{ mol}$. Minimum required mass: $m = 0.1741\text{ mol} \times 84.0\text{ g/mol} \approx 14.63\text{ g} \approx 14.6\text{ g}$. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Metal carbides are classified into methanides, acetylides, and sesquicarbides based on the constitution of their carbon anions. Reflecting their diagonal relationship, both beryllium carbide ($\text{Be}_2\text{C}$) and aluminum carbide ($\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$) are methanides containing isolated $\text{C}^{4-}$ anions. In an isotopic labeling experiment, $0.100\text{ mol}$ of pure $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ and $0.100\text{ mol}$ of pure $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$ are separately treated with an excess of deuterium oxide ($\text{D}_2\text{O}$, heavy water). Taking atomic masses as $\text{C} = 12.0\text{ g/mol}$ and $\text{D} = 2.0\text{ g/mol}$, identify the deuterated hydrocarbon gas formed in both reactions, and calculate the individual masses (in grams) of this hydrocarbon evolved from the beryllium carbide and aluminum carbide reactions, respectively.
options: A) $\text{CD}_4$; $2.00\text{ g}$ from $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ and $6.00\text{ g}$ from $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$
B) $\text{C}_2\text{D}_2$ from $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ ($2.80\text{ g}$) and $\text{CD}_4$ from $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$ ($6.00\text{ g}$)
C) $\text{CD}_4$ from $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ ($2.00\text{ g}$) and $\text{C}_3\text{D}_4$ from $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$ ($4.40\text{ g}$)
D) $\text{CD}_4$; $1.60\text{ g}$ from $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ and $4.80\text{ g}$ from $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Identify the nature of the carbide anions. Both $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ and $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$ are ionic methanides containing discrete $\text{C}^{4-}$ ions, unlike $\text{CaC}_2$ (acetylide, $\text{C}_2^{2-}$) and $\text{Mg}_2\text{C}_3$ (allylenide, $\text{C}_3^{4-}$). Step 2: The balanced equations for deuterolysis are: $\text{Be}_2\text{C} + 4\text{D}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Be(OD)}_2 + \text{CD}_4(g)$ and $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 + 12\text{D}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{Al(OD)}_3 + 3\text{CD}_4(g)$. Both reactions generate deuteriomethane ($\text{CD}_4$). Step 3: The molar mass of $\text{CD}_4$ is $12.0 + 4(2.0) = 20.0\text{ g/mol}$. From $0.100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Be}_2\text{C}$, moles of $\text{CD}_4 = 0.100\text{ mol}$, yielding mass $= 0.100 \times 20.0 = 2.00\text{ g}$. Step 4: From $0.100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$, moles of $\text{CD}_4 = 3 \times 0.100 = 0.300\text{ mol}$, yielding mass $= 0.300 \times 20.0 = 6.00\text{ g}$. Option D incorrectly uses the molar mass of undeuterated methane ($16.0\text{ g/mol}$). Option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Owing to the high polarizing power of the tiny $\text{Li}^+$ cation ($r = 76\text{ pm}$), lithium halides exhibit distinct chemical anomalies that parallel magnesium halides rather than heavier alkali metal halides. Consider the following statements:
(1) Lithium fluoride ($\text{LiF}$) has very low solubility in water at $298\text{ K}$ because its exceptionally high lattice enthalpy ($1036\text{ kJ/mol}$) overcomes its hydration enthalpy.
(2) Lithium chloride is highly deliquescent and readily crystallizes from aqueous solution as a dihydrate ($\text{LiCl}\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$), mirroring $\text{MgCl}_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, whereas $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{KCl}$ do not form hydrates at room temperature.
(3) The covalent character of lithium halides increases in the sequence $\text{LiF} < \text{LiCl} < \text{LiBr} < \text{LiI}$ due to the increasing polarizability of the halide anions.
(4) Among all alkali metal fluorides, $\text{LiF}$ possesses the highest melting point.
(5) Unlike $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{KCl}$, lithium chloride is appreciably soluble in organic polar solvents such as ethanol, acetone, and pyridine.
(6) Solid anhydrous lithium hydrogen carbonate ($\text{LiHCO}_3$) can be isolated at room temperature as a stable crystalline solid.
Determine the total number of statements that are scientifically CORRECT.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Statement (1) is TRUE: The low solubility of $\text{LiF}$ in water is caused by its very high lattice enthalpy ($1036\text{ kJ/mol}$) resulting from the contact of two small, hard ions ($\text{Li}^+$ and $\text{F}^-$). Step 2: Statement (2) is TRUE: Small $\text{Li}^+$ has high hydration enthalpy, enabling crystallization as $\text{LiCl}\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, exactly like $\text{MgCl}_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Step 3: Statement (3) is TRUE: Applying Fajans' rules, increasing anion radius and polarizability from $\text{F}^-$ to $\text{I}^-$ enhances electron cloud distortion by $\text{Li}^+$, progressively increasing covalent character: $\text{LiF} < \text{LiCl} < \text{LiBr} < \text{LiI}$. Step 4: Statement (4) is FALSE: Although $\text{LiF}$ has the highest lattice energy, $\text{NaF}$ has the highest melting point ($993^\circ\text{C}$ vs $848^\circ\text{C}$ for $\text{LiF}$) because significant covalent polarization in $\text{LiF}$ weakens the ionic crystal lattice. Step 5: Statement (5) is TRUE: Substantial covalent character in $\text{LiCl}$ imparts high solubility in organic donor solvents like ethanol and pyridine. Step 6: Statement (6) is FALSE: Lithium hydrogen carbonate does not exist in the solid state due to high polarizing power of $\text{Li}^+$, existing only in aqueous solution. Statements (1), (2), (3), and (5) are CORRECT, giving exactly 4 correct statements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In dilute solutions of alkali metals in anhydrous liquid ammonia at $-33^\circ\text{C}$, the valence electron separates from the alkali cation and is trapped in a microscopic solvent cavity created by displaced ammonia molecules. In the cavity model, this ammoniated electron $e^-(\text{am})$ occupies a spherical void with an effective cavity radius of $r_{\text{cav}} = 3.30\text{ \AA}$ ($3.30 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}$). Taking Avogadro's constant as $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $\pi \approx 3.1416$, calculate the theoretical molar void volume $V_{\text{void}}$ (in $\text{cm}^3/\text{mol}$) occupied by one mole of these electron cavities. If cation electrostriction contracts the surrounding solvent by $25.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$ per mole of $\text{Na}^+$, determine the net apparent molar volume change $\Delta V_{\text{net}}$ (in $\text{cm}^3/\text{mol}$) observed upon dissolving sodium metal.
options: A) $V_{\text{void}} \approx 90.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$ and $\Delta V_{\text{net}} = +65.0\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$
B) $V_{\text{void}} \approx 90.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$ and $\Delta V_{\text{net}} = -65.0\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$
C) $V_{\text{void}} \approx 22.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$ and $\Delta V_{\text{net}} = -3.0\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$
D) $V_{\text{void}} \approx 181.4\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$ and $\Delta V_{\text{net}} = +155.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: The volume of a single spherical cavity of radius $r_{\text{cav}} = 3.30 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm}$ is: $v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}(3.1416)(3.30 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm})^3 = \frac{4}{3}(3.1416)(3.5937 \times 10^{-23}) \approx 1.5053 \times 10^{-22}\text{ cm}^3$. Step 2: The total void volume contributed by one mole of such electron cavities is obtained by multiplying by Avogadro's number: $V_{\text{void}} = N_A \cdot v = (6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1})(1.5053 \times 10^{-22}\text{ cm}^3) \approx 90.65\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol} \approx 90.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$. Distractor C arises from confusing radius with diameter ($1.65\text{ \AA}$), and D results from multiplying by an extra factor of 2. Step 3: Electrostriction of solvent dipoles around the $\text{Na}^+$ cation exerts a contracting effect of $-25.7\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$. Hence, the net apparent molar volume change for the dissolved system is: $\Delta V_{\text{net}} = V_{\text{void}} + \Delta V_{\text{electrostriction}} = 90.7 - 25.7 = +65.0\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$. Therefore, the large positive volume expansion explains why alkali metal-liquid ammonia solutions have an unusually low density compared to pure ammonia, confirming option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Alkali metals dissolve reversibly in anhydrous liquid ammonia across a wide concentration range without chemical decomposition under rigorously pure conditions. Which of the following statements regarding the physical, magnetic, and spectroscopic properties of these solutions is/are CORRECT?
options: A) In dilute solutions ($< 0.1\text{ M}$), the system exhibits an intense blue coloration with a broad electronic absorption maximum near $1500\text{ nm}$ in the near-infrared, assigned to the $1s \to 2p$-like excitation of the cavity-bound solvated electron

B) Dilute solutions exhibit strong paramagnetism corresponding to an effective spin-only magnetic moment $\mu_{\text{eff}} \approx 1.73\text{ B.M.}$ per dissolved metal atom, and conduct electricity primarily via migration and tunneling of ammoniated electrons

C) When the metal concentration exceeds $3.0\text{ M}$, the solution transitions into a bronze-colored liquid with metallic luster, electrical conductivity comparable to molten metals, and sharply reduced magnetic susceptibility due to spin pairing: $2e^-(\text{am}) \rightleftharpoons e_2^{2-}(\text{am})$

D) In the presence of finely divided iron(III) oxide ($\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$) or trace transition metal impurities, the blue solution rapidly bleaches with stoichiometric liberation of $\text{H}_2(g)$ and precipitation of metal amide ($\text{MNH}_2$)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Statement A is CORRECT: In dilute solutions, the solvated electron $e^-(\text{am})$ occupies a cavity of $3.3\text{ \AA}$ radius. Its broad optical absorption spectrum exhibits a peak near $1500\text{ nm}$ ($0.8\text{ eV}$) with a tail extending into the red visible region, giving the solution its intense deep blue color. Step 2: Statement B is CORRECT: Free unpaired solvated electrons possess spin $S = 1/2$, yielding a Curie-type paramagnetism with $\mu_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\text{ B.M.}$. The electrical conductivity is exceptionally high because the cavity electron has high mobility via quantum mechanical tunneling. Step 3: Statement C is CORRECT: Above $\sim 3\text{ M}$, ammoniated electrons pair their spins to form diamagnetic bielectron species $e_2^{2-}(\text{am})$, reducing magnetic susceptibility. Delocalization of valence electrons into an expanded conduction band imparts bronze luster and metallic conductivity ($10^4\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$). Step 4: Statement D is CORRECT: Dissolution is thermodynamically metastable; addition of catalysts like $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ accelerates the redox reaction: $2\text{M} + 2\text{NH}_3 \to 2\text{MNH}_2 + \text{H}_2(g)$, discharging the blue color. All statements A, B, C, and D are therefore correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Determine the standard enthalpy of formation ($\Delta H_f^\circ$) of crystalline potassium superoxide, $\text{KO}_2(s)$, from the following standard thermochemical data at $298\text{ K}$:
- Standard enthalpy of sublimation of metallic potassium: $\Delta H_{\text{sub}}^\circ(\text{K}) = +89.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
- First ionization enthalpy of potassium: $IE_1(\text{K}) = +419.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
- Standard bond dissociation enthalpy of dioxygen: $D(\text{O}_2) = +498.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
- First electron affinity of dioxygen: $\Delta H_{\text{EA1}}(\text{O}_2) = -43.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ for $\text{O}_2(g) + e^- \to \text{O}_2^-(g)$
- Lattice enthalpy of $\text{KO}_2(s)$ defined as $\text{K}^+(g) + \text{O}_2^-(g) \to \text{KO}_2(s)$: $U_{\text{lat}} = -749.0\text{ kJ/mol}$.
options: A) $-284.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
B) $-35.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
C) $+214.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
D) $-198.0\text{ kJ/mol}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: The standard formation reaction for potassium superoxide is: $\text{K}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to \text{KO}_2(s)$. Step 2: Construct the Born-Haber thermochemical cycle: Sublimation: $\text{K}(s) \to \text{K}(g)$, with $\Delta H_1 = \Delta H_{\text{sub}}^\circ(\text{K}) = +89.0\text{ kJ/mol}$. Ionization: $\text{K}(g) \to \text{K}^+(g) + e^-$, with $\Delta H_2 = IE_1(\text{K}) = +419.0\text{ kJ/mol}$. Electron attachment to molecular oxygen: $\text{O}_2(g) + e^- \to \text{O}_2^-(g)$, with $\Delta H_3 = \Delta H_{\text{EA1}}(\text{O}_2) = -43.0\text{ kJ/mol}$. (Crucially, the $\text{O-O}$ covalent bond is NOT cleaved in superoxide formation, so the bond dissociation enthalpy $D(\text{O}_2) = +498.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ must NOT be included in the cycle). Step 3: Lattice condensation: $\text{K}^+(g) + \text{O}_2^-(g) \to \text{KO}_2(s)$, with $\Delta H_4 = U_{\text{lat}} = -749.0\text{ kJ/mol}$. Step 4: Applying Hess's law: $\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{KO}_2, s) = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3 + \Delta H_4 = 89.0 + 419.0 + (-43.0) + (-749.0) = 508.0 - 792.0 = -284.0\text{ kJ/mol}$. Erroneously adding $\frac{1}{2}D(\text{O}_2) = +249.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ yields $-35.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ (Option B), adding full $D(\text{O}_2)$ yields $+214.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ (Option C), and inverting the sign of electron affinity yields $-198.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ (Option D). Option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following solid binary oxygen-containing compounds of s-block elements:
(1) $\text{BaO}_2$
(2) $\text{KO}_2$
(3) $\text{CsO}_2$
(4) $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$
(5) $\text{Li}_2\text{O}$
(6) $\text{RbO}_2$
(7) $\text{CaO}$
Let $N_p$ be the number of compounds in this list that exhibit PARAMAGNETISM at room temperature. Let $S_b$ be the sum of the dioxygen anion formal bond orders for all compounds in the list that contain either a peroxide ($\text{O}_2^{2-}$) or superoxide ($\text{O}_2^-$) anion. Determine the integer value of $(10 \times S_b) + N_p$.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Analyze the electronic structures using Molecular Orbital theory for dioxygen anions: For superoxide $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17$ electrons): valence configuration is $\sigma_{2p_z}^2\pi_{2p_x}^2\pi_{2p_y}^2(\pi^*_{2p_x})^2(\pi^*_{2p_y})^1$. It has 1 unpaired electron ($S = 1/2$), making it PARAMAGNETIC, with formal bond order $= \frac{8 - 5}{2} = 1.5$. For peroxide $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18$ electrons): valence configuration is $\sigma_{2p_z}^2\pi_{2p_x}^2\pi_{2p_y}^2(\pi^*_{2p_x})^2(\pi^*_{2p_y})^2$. All electrons are paired, making it DIAMAGNETIC, with formal bond order $= \frac{8 - 6}{2} = 1.0$. For normal oxides ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}$, $\text{CaO}$): they contain discrete oxide $\text{O}^{2-}$ ($10$ electrons, closed-shell neon configuration, diamagnetic) and have no dioxygen bond. Step 2: Identify paramagnetic compounds: The superoxides are $\text{KO}_2$, $\text{CsO}_2$, and $\text{RbO}_2$. Hence, $N_p = 3$. Step 3: Identify compounds with dioxygen anions and sum their bond orders: $\text{BaO}_2$ (peroxide, $1.0$), $\text{KO}_2$ (superoxide, $1.5$), $\text{CsO}_2$ (superoxide, $1.5$), $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ (peroxide, $1.0$), and $\text{RbO}_2$ (superoxide, $1.5$). Therefore, $S_b = 1.0 + 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.0 + 1.5 = 6.5$. Step 4: Computing $(10 \times S_b) + N_p$: $(10 \times 6.5) + 3 = 65 + 3 = 68$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Alkali metals dissolved in liquid ammonia serve as versatile reagents whose reaction pathways depend critically on the acidity of organic substrates. When $0.100\text{ mol}$ of sodium metal is reacted with an excess of 1-butyne ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$) in anhydrous liquid ammonia at $-33^\circ\text{C}$, a gas is evolved quantitatively. Simultaneously, when sodium in liquid ammonia is reacted with an internal alkyne such as 2-butyne ($\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CCH}_3$), reduction occurs stereoselectively. Calculate the volume of dry gas (in liters at STP, $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1.00\text{ atm}$, molar volume $22.4\text{ L/mol}$) evolved from the 1-butyne reaction, and identify the stereochemical configuration of the alkene formed from the 2-butyne reduction.
options: A) $1.12\text{ L}$ of $\text{H}_2(g)$; trans-2-butene ((E)-but-2-ene)
B) $2.24\text{ L}$ of $\text{H}_2(g)$; cis-2-butene ((Z)-but-2-ene)
C) $1.12\text{ L}$ of butane gas; trans-2-butene ((E)-but-2-ene)
D) $2.24\text{ L}$ of butane gas; cis-2-butene ((Z)-but-2-ene)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Terminal alkynes contain an acidic sp-hybridized C-H proton ($pK_a \approx 25$). When treated with sodium in liquid ammonia, 1-butyne undergoes acid-base proton reduction rather than triple bond hydrogenation: $2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{CH} + 2\text{Na} \to 2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2(g)$. Step 2: Moles of $\text{H}_2(g)$ evolved from $0.100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Na}$ is: $n(\text{H}_2) = \frac{0.100\text{ mol}}{2} = 0.050\text{ mol}$. The volume of $\text{H}_2(g)$ at STP is: $V = 0.050\text{ mol} \times 22.4\text{ L/mol} = 1.12\text{ L}$. Distractor B results from failing to divide by the stoichiometric coefficient 2. Step 3: For internal alkynes like 2-butyne, there is no acidic terminal proton. The solvated electron undergoes Birch-type single electron transfer (SET) to generate a radical anion intermediate. Trans-inversion occurs to minimize steric and electrostatic repulsion between the two methyl groups before protonation by $\text{NH}_3$, selectively yielding the trans-alkene (trans-2-butene or (E)-but-2-ene), in contrast to Lindlar's heterogeneous hydrogenation which yields the cis isomer. Thus, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The Kapustinskii equation indicates that the lattice enthalpy of an ionic crystal scales inversely with the sum of ionic radii: $U_{\text{lat}} \propto \frac{\nu z_+ z_-}{r_+ + r_-}$. In the combustion of alkali metals with excess oxygen, lithium forms exclusively the normal oxide $\text{Li}_2\text{O}$, while cesium forms the superoxide $\text{CsO}_2$. Given ionic radii: $r(\text{Li}^+) = 76\text{ pm}$, $r(\text{Cs}^+) = 167\text{ pm}$, $r(\text{O}^{2-}) = 140\text{ pm}$, and $r(\text{O}_2^-) = 180\text{ pm}$, which thermodynamic explanation correctly accounts for this product differentiation?
options: A) The small radius of $\text{Li}^+$ generates an extraordinarily large lattice enthalpy with small $\text{O}^{2-}$ ($U_{\text{lat}} > 3300\text{ kJ/mol}$), readily compensating the high energetic cost of $\text{O-O}$ bond cleavage and the endothermic second electron affinity of oxygen, whereas for large $\text{Cs}^+$, oxide lattice energy drops sharply, making formation of $\text{CsO}_2$ (where the $\text{O-O}$ bond remains intact) thermodynamically favored
B) The high ionization energy of cesium prevents it from releasing enough electrons to reduce oxygen beyond the $-1/2$ oxidation state
C) The small lithium cation is too large to fit into the crystal lattice of a superoxide, leading to steric repulsion between superoxide anions
D) Superoxides are stabilized exclusively by covalent $\pi$-backbonding, which is maximal for cesium due to its available 5d empty orbitals
questions.explanation: Step 1: Generating the oxide anion $\text{O}^{2-}$ from $\text{O}_2(g)$ requires paying the bond dissociation energy $D(\text{O}_2) = +498\text{ kJ/mol}$ plus the strongly endothermic second electron affinity $\text{O}^- + e^- \to \text{O}^{2-}$ ($\Delta H \approx +844\text{ kJ/mol}$). Step 2: For lithium, $r(\text{Li}^+) + r(\text{O}^{2-}) = 76 + 140 = 216\text{ pm}$. The very small internuclear distance and the $-2$ anion charge result in an immense lattice energy for $\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ ($U_{\text{lat}} \approx 3340\text{ kJ/mol}$), which comfortably overcomes all energetic penalties to maximize thermodynamic stability. Step 3: For cesium, $r(\text{Cs}^+) + r(\text{O}^{2-}) = 167 + 140 = 307\text{ pm}$. The large internuclear distance reduces the oxide lattice energy to $\approx 2350\text{ kJ/mol}$. This diminished lattice gain can no longer compensate the bond cleavage and $\text{EA}_2$ penalties relative to forming $\text{CsO}_2$, where the $\text{O-O}$ bond is preserved and the first electron affinity is exothermic ($-43\text{ kJ/mol}$). Step 4: Furthermore, large cations have low surface charge density, stabilizing large polyatomic anions like $\text{O}_2^-$ without inducing polarization-induced lattice destabilization. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Alkali metal peroxides and superoxides are widely deployed in closed-circuit breathing systems (such as in aerospace capsules and submarines) due to their coupled capacity to scrub carbon dioxide and regenerate oxygen. Which of the following statements regarding their chemical reactivity is/are CORRECT?
options: A) In the complete reaction of potassium superoxide with carbon dioxide to form potassium carbonate: $4\text{KO}_2(s) + 2\text{CO}_2(g) \to 2\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g)$, the stoichiometric respiratory quotient (ratio of moles of $\text{CO}_2$ absorbed to moles of $\text{O}_2$ released) is exactly $2/3 \approx 0.67$

B) In the reaction of $\text{KO}_2$ with water: $2\text{KO}_2(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 2\text{KOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2(aq) + \text{O}_2(g)$, oxygen undergoes a formal disproportionation from oxidation state $-1/2$ to $0$ (in $\text{O}_2$) and $-1$ (in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$)

C) Sodium peroxide reacts smoothly with ice-cold dilute sulfuric acid ($0^\circ\text{C}$) to produce an aqueous solution of hydrogen peroxide without evolution of oxygen gas: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2(s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \to \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2(aq)$

D) If moisture and excess carbon dioxide react with $\text{KO}_2$ to precipitate potassium hydrogen carbonate: $4\text{KO}_2(s) + 4\text{CO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 4\text{KHCO}_3(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g)$, the ratio of $\text{CO}_2$ scrubbed to $\text{O}_2$ released is $4/3 \approx 1.33$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Statement A is CORRECT: For $4\text{KO}_2 + 2\text{CO}_2 \to 2\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 + 3\text{O}_2$, the ratio of $\text{CO}_2$ consumed to $\text{O}_2$ generated is $\frac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$. Step 2: Statement B is CORRECT: The superoxide ion has oxygen in oxidation state $-1/2$. In $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, oxygen has oxidation state $-1$ (reduction, gaining $1/2$ electron per oxygen), and in $\text{O}_2$, oxygen has oxidation state $0$ (oxidation, losing $1/2$ electron per oxygen). This constitutes a classic disproportionation redox process. Step 3: Statement C is CORRECT: Because $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ is a salt of the weak diprotic acid $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, cold dilute mineral acids protonate the peroxide ion to yield aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ quantitatively without thermal decomposition into $\text{O}_2$. Step 4: Statement D is CORRECT: When excess $\text{CO}_2$ and moisture drive conversion to bicarbonate, $4\text{KO}_2 + 4\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{KHCO}_3 + 3\text{O}_2$, the molar ratio of $\text{CO}_2$ absorbed to $\text{O}_2$ released is exactly $4/3 \approx 1.33$. Statements A, B, C, and D are all correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: A $5.253\text{ g}$ dry solid mixture containing only pure sodium peroxide ($\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$, molar mass $78.0\text{ g/mol}$) and pure potassium superoxide ($\text{KO}_2$, molar mass $71.1\text{ g/mol}$) is treated carefully with an excess of ice-cold aqueous sulfuric acid. The initial dissolution produces an aqueous solution of hydrogen peroxide and evolves exactly $336\text{ mL}$ of dry oxygen gas ($\text{O}_2$) measured at STP ($0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1.00\text{ atm}$, where molar volume is $22.4\text{ L/mol}$). The resulting homogeneous acidic solution is subsequently titrated against standard $0.200\text{ M}\ \text{KMnO}_4$ solution: $2\text{MnO}_4^- + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 6\text{H}^+ \to 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{O}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Determine the total volume (in $\text{mL}$, rounded to the nearest integer) of $0.200\text{ M}\ \text{KMnO}_4$ consumed in the titration.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Write the stoichiometric dissolution equations in cold dilute acid: For sodium peroxide: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ (no $\text{O}_2$ evolved). For potassium superoxide: $2\text{KO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{O}_2(g)$. Step 2: Calculate moles of evolved $\text{O}_2(g)$: $n(\text{O}_2) = \frac{0.336\text{ L}}{22.4\text{ L/mol}} = 0.0150\text{ mol}$. Since $2\text{ mol}\ \text{KO}_2$ produce $1\text{ mol}\ \text{O}_2$, the moles of $\text{KO}_2$ present is: $n(\text{KO}_2) = 2 \times 0.0150 = 0.0300\text{ mol}$. Step 3: Determine mass and moles of $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$: Mass of $\text{KO}_2 = 0.0300\text{ mol} \times 71.1\text{ g/mol} = 2.133\text{ g}$. Mass of $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 = 5.253\text{ g} - 2.133\text{ g} = 3.120\text{ g}$. Moles of $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 = \frac{3.120\text{ g}}{78.0\text{ g/mol}} = 0.0400\text{ mol}$. Step 4: Total moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ formed: From $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$: $0.0400\text{ mol}$. From $\text{KO}_2$: $\frac{0.0300}{2} = 0.0150\text{ mol}$. Total $n(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2) = 0.0400 + 0.0150 = 0.0550\text{ mol}$. Step 5: Stoichiometry of permanganate redox titration: $2\text{ mol}\ \text{KMnO}_4 \equiv 5\text{ mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$. Moles of $\text{KMnO}_4 = \frac{2}{5} \times 0.0550\text{ mol} = 0.0220\text{ mol}$. Volume of $0.200\text{ M}\ \text{KMnO}_4$: $V = \frac{0.0220\text{ mol}}{0.200\text{ mol/L}} = 0.110\text{ L} = 110\text{ mL}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In liquid ammonia at $-33^\circ\text{C}$, paramagnetic solvated electrons exist in dynamic equilibrium with diamagnetic spin-paired electron dimers: $2e^-(\text{am}) \rightleftharpoons e_2^{2-}(\text{am})$, with equilibrium constant $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{[e_2^{2-}]}{[e^-]^2}$. At a total analytical concentration of dissolved sodium $C_0 = 0.050\text{ M}$, static magnetic susceptibility measurements establish that exactly $40.0\%$ of the valence electrons are paired as dimers, while $60.0\%$ remain as free paramagnetic solvated electrons. Determine the numerical value of $K_{\text{eq}}$ (in $\text{M}^{-1}$), and calculate the percentage of valence electrons that exist as free solvated electrons when the solution is diluted tenfold to $C_0' = 0.0050\text{ M}$.
questions.explanation: Step 1: The electron balance is given by $[e^-] + 2[e_2^{2-}] = C_0 = 0.050\text{ M}$. At $C_0 = 0.050\text{ M}$, $40.0\%$ of electrons are in dimers: $2[e_2^{2-}] = 0.400 \times 0.050 = 0.020\text{ M} \implies [e_2^{2-}] = 0.010\text{ M}$. The remaining $60.0\%$ are monomers: $[e^-] = 0.600 \times 0.050 = 0.030\text{ M}$. Step 2: The equilibrium constant is: $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{[e_2^{2-}]}{[e^-]^2} = \frac{0.010\text{ M}}{(0.030\text{ M})^2} = \frac{0.010}{0.0009} = \frac{100}{9} \approx 11.11\text{ M}^{-1}$. Step 3: At tenfold dilution, $C_0' = 0.0050\text{ M}$. Let $\alpha$ be the fraction of electrons existing as free monomeric $e^-$. Then $[e^-] = \alpha C_0' = 0.0050\alpha$, and $[e_2^{2-}] = \frac{(1 - \alpha)C_0'}{2} = 0.0025(1 - \alpha)$. Step 4: Substituting into the equilibrium expression: $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{0.0025(1 - \alpha)}{(0.0050\alpha)^2} = \frac{0.0025(1 - \alpha)}{2.5 \times 10^{-5}\alpha^2} = \frac{100(1 - \alpha)}{\alpha^2}$. Equating to $\frac{100}{9}$: $\frac{100}{9} = \frac{100(1 - \alpha)}{\alpha^2} \implies \alpha^2 = 9(1 - \alpha) \implies \alpha^2 + 9\alpha - 9 = 0$. Step 5: Solving the quadratic equation for positive root: $\alpha = \frac{-9 + \sqrt{81 - 4(1)(-9)}}{2} = \frac{-9 + \sqrt{117}}{2} = \frac{-9 + 10.8166}{2} \approx 0.9083 \approx 90.8\%$. Dilution drives dissociation of the dimer, increasing monomer percentage from $60.0\%$ to $90.8\%$, confirming option A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When dry powdered potassium hydroxide or potassium metal is treated with an ozonized oxygen stream at low temperature ($-15^\circ\text{C}$), deep orange-red potassium ozonide ($\text{KO}_3$) is synthesized. The ozonide radical anion, $\text{O}_3^-$, possesses 19 valence electrons and is isoelectronic with chlorine dioxide ($\text{ClO}_2$) and nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$). Which of the following statements concerning potassium ozonide and its comparative chemistry with $\text{KO}_2$ and $\text{K}_2\text{O}_2$ is FALSE?
options: A) The ozonide anion $\text{O}_3^-$ possesses a bent open geometry with $C_{2v}$ point group symmetry and a bond angle of approximately $113^\circ$, exhibiting paramagnetism with one unpaired electron residing in an antibonding $\pi^*$ molecular orbital
B) Thermal decomposition of solid $\text{KO}_3$ proceeds spontaneously at room temperature to yield potassium superoxide and dioxygen: $2\text{KO}_3(s) \to 2\text{KO}_2(s) + \text{O}_2(g)$

C) Hydrolysis of $\text{KO}_3$ in aqueous medium generates potassium hydroxide and oxygen gas with transient intermediate formation of hydroxyl radicals: $4\text{KO}_3(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 4\text{KOH}(aq) + 5\text{O}_2(g)$
D) Potassium ozonide is completely diamagnetic because the three oxygen atoms form a closed cyclic cyclopropane-like triangular ring in which all electron spins are paired
questions.explanation: Step 1: Inspect the molecular orbital structure of the ozonide ion $\text{O}_3^-$: It has $3 \times 6 + 1 = 19$ valence electrons. According to Walsh diagrams and MO theory, it adopts a bent open chain structure ($C_{2v}$ symmetry) with an O-O-O bond angle of $\approx 113.5^\circ$ and O-O bond length of $1.34\text{ \AA}$. The unpaired electron occupies the highest half-filled $1a_2$ antibonding $\pi^*$ orbital. Statement A is TRUE. Step 2: Thermal decomposition of $\text{KO}_3$ occurs above $0^\circ\text{C}$ to produce $\text{KO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$: $2\text{KO}_3 \to 2\text{KO}_2 + \text{O}_2$, releasing oxygen. Statement B is TRUE. Step 3: Dissolution in water produces vigorous effervescence: $4\text{KO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{KOH} + 5\text{O}_2$, proceeding via radical mechanisms. Statement C is TRUE. Step 4: Statement D is FALSE: The ozonide ion is NOT a cyclic ring, and it is definitely NOT diamagnetic; it possesses an odd electron and shows paramagnetism with a spin-only magnetic moment $\mu = 1.73\text{ B.M.}$. Therefore, statement D is the false statement and is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
The host-guest complexation of alkali metal cations by 18-crown-6 in anhydrous methanol at $298.15\text{ K}$ follows the homogeneous equilibrium: $\text{M}^+(solv) + \text{18C6}(solv) \rightleftharpoons [\text{M}(\text{18C6})]^+(solv)$. The standard thermodynamic parameters are:
- For $\text{Na}^+$ ($r_+ = 102\text{ pm}$): $\Delta H^\circ = -35.00\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -52.00\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$
- For $\text{K}^+$ ($r_+ = 138\text{ pm}$): $\Delta H^\circ = -56.00\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -74.00\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$.
Taking the gas constant as $R = 8.314\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$, calculate the thermodynamic selectivity ratio $S = \frac{K_f(\text{K}^+)}{K_f(\text{Na}^+)}$ at $298.15\text{ K}$, and identify the physical structural factor that determines this pronounced selectivity.
options: A) $S \approx 339$; the cavity diameter of 18-crown-6 ($2.6\text{--}3.2\text{ \AA}$) matches the diameter of $\text{K}^+$ ($2.76\text{ \AA}$), maximizing all six ion-dipole interactions without ligand conformational strain
B) $S \approx 2.95 \times 10^{-3}$; $\text{Na}^+$ binds more tightly due to its higher surface charge density
C) $S \approx 339$; the complexation of $\text{K}^+$ is driven primarily by a favorable positive entropy of complexation
D) $S \approx 58.3$; selectivity is dictated exclusively by the lower desolvation enthalpy of potassium in methanol
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compute the standard Gibbs energy of complexation for both cations using $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$: For $\text{Na}^+$: $\Delta G^\circ(\text{Na}^+) = -35000\text{ J/mol} - (298.15\text{ K})(-52.00\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}) = -35000 + 15503.8 = -19496.2\text{ J/mol} = -19.50\text{ kJ/mol}$. For $\text{K}^+$: $\Delta G^\circ(\text{K}^+) = -56000\text{ J/mol} - (298.15\text{ K})(-74.00\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}) = -56000 + 22063.1 = -33936.9\text{ J/mol} = -33.94\text{ kJ/mol}$. Step 2: The difference in Gibbs energy is: $\Delta\Delta G^\circ = \Delta G^\circ(\text{K}^+) - \Delta G^\circ(\text{Na}^+) = -33936.9 - (-19496.2) = -14440.7\text{ J/mol}$. Step 3: The selectivity ratio of formation constants is given by: $S = \frac{K_f(\text{K}^+)}{K_f(\text{Na}^+)} = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta\Delta G^\circ}{RT}\right) = \exp\left(\frac{14440.7\text{ J/mol}}{(8.314\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)})(298.15\text{ K})}\right) = \exp(5.8257) \approx 338.9 \approx 339$. Step 4: The 18-crown-6 cavity has a diameter of $2.6\text{--}3.2\text{ \AA}$. The diameter of $\text{K}^+$ ($2 \times 1.38\text{ \AA} = 2.76\text{ \AA}$) fits snugly into this cavity, allowing planar coordination by all six ether oxygens with optimum $\text{K}^+\cdots\text{O}$ bond distances and minimal conformational strain. In contrast, $\text{Na}^+$ ($d = 2.04\text{ \AA}$) is too small, forcing the ligand to fold or undergo conformational distortion, which results in a substantially less exothermic enthalpy of binding ($\Delta H^\circ$ is less negative by $21\text{ kJ/mol}$). Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The isolation of stable crystalline alkalides (salts containing genuine alkali metal anions $\text{M}^-$) and electrides (salts containing trapped electrons $e^-$ as counter-anions) was achieved by James Dye using macrobicyclic cryptands. Consider the synthesis of crystalline potasside via: $2\text{K}(s) + [2.2.2]\text{-crypt} \to [\text{K}(\text{crypt-2.2.2})]^+\text{K}^-(s)$ in anhydrous ethylamine. Which of the following statements regarding alkalides and electrides is/are CORRECT?
options: A) The cryptate effect provides an extraordinarily high complex formation constant for $[\text{K}(\text{crypt-2.2.2})]^+$ ($K_f > 10^{10}\text{ M}^{-1}$), which provides the critical thermodynamic driving force needed to overcome the endothermic disproportionation $2\text{K}(s) \to \text{K}^+(g) + \text{K}^-(g)$

B) In crystalline $[\text{K}(\text{crypt-2.2.2})]^+\text{K}^-$, the potasside anion $\text{K}^-$ has the closed-shell valence electron configuration $[\text{Ar}]4s^2$, is diamagnetic, and has an ionic radius ($r \approx 2.3\text{ \AA}$) significantly larger than both neutral metallic potassium and $\text{K}^+$

C) In crystalline electrides such as $[\text{Cs}(\text{18-crown-6})_2]^+ e^-$, the anionic electron resides in empty interstitial crystal cavities rather than on an atomic nucleus, behaving as an anionic spin center that displays temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility

D) In crystalline $[\text{K}(\text{crypt-2.2.2})]^+\text{K}^-$, potassium atoms exist simultaneously in two distinct formal oxidation states of $+1$ (encapsulated within the cage) and $-1$ (occupying external anionic lattice sites)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Statement A is CORRECT: Monocyclic crown ethers cannot prevent the back-reaction because their complexation constants are insufficient. The 3D bicyclic architecture of [2.2.2]-cryptand provides three-dimensional encapsulating chelation (the cryptate effect), releasing sufficient solvation/lattice free energy to drive the otherwise endothermic disproportionation $2\text{K} \to \text{K}^+ + \text{K}^-$. Step 2: Statement B is CORRECT: The potasside anion $\text{K}^-$ has acquired a second electron in its $4s$ subshell ($[\text{Ar}]4s^2$), giving a completely filled, spherically symmetric orbital with paired spins (diamagnetic). Mutual electron-electron repulsion in the diffuse outer $4s$ orbital drastically expands its ionic radius ($r \approx 2.3\text{ \AA}$ vs $1.38\text{ \AA}$ for $\text{K}^+$). Step 3: Statement C is CORRECT: In electrides, empty lattice voids created between bulky complexed cations trap isolated electrons, creating stoichiometric F-center analogues that display magnetic exchange couplings. Step 4: Statement D is CORRECT: Single crystal X-ray diffraction and NMR confirm two completely distinct chemical environments: $+1$ in the central cryptate core and $-1$ in the lattice anion positions. All four statements are correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Potassium permanganate ($\text{KMnO}_4$) is completely insoluble in nonpolar benzene. Addition of dicyclohexano-18-crown-6 ($\text{DC18C6}$) solubilizes $\text{KMnO}_4$ into benzene, generating 'purple benzene' capable of oxidizing alkenes. In a liquid-liquid extraction system at $298\text{ K}$ with equal volumes of aqueous and benzene phases, the extraction equilibrium is represented by: $\text{K}^+(aq) + \text{MnO}_4^-(aq) + \text{DC18C6}(org) \rightleftharpoons [\text{K}(\text{DC18C6})]^+\text{MnO}_4^-(org)$, with extraction constant $K_{\text{ex}} = 30.86\text{ M}^{-2}$. If the initial concentration of $\text{KMnO}_4$ in the aqueous phase is $0.100\text{ M}$ and the initial concentration of $\text{DC18C6}$ in the benzene phase is $0.050\text{ M}$, determine the equilibrium concentration of permanganate extracted into the benzene phase (in $\text{mM}$), and calculate the percentage of initial crown ether that is bound to potassium at equilibrium.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Set up the equilibrium mass balance expressions: Let $x$ be the molar concentration of $[\text{K}(\text{DC18C6})]^+\text{MnO}_4^-$ in the organic benzene phase at equilibrium. Because phase volumes are equal ($V_{\text{aq}} = V_{\text{org}}$), the depletion in the aqueous phase equals the formation in the organic phase. Thus: $[\text{K}^+]_{\text{aq}} = 0.100 - x$, $[\text{MnO}_4^-]_{\text{aq}} = 0.100 - x$, $[\text{DC18C6}]_{\text{org}} = 0.050 - x$, and $[[\text{K}(\text{DC18C6})]^+\text{MnO}_4^-]_{\text{org}} = x$. Step 2: The extraction equilibrium expression is: $K_{\text{ex}} = \frac{x}{(0.100 - x)^2(0.050 - x)} = 30.86\text{ M}^{-2}$. Step 3: Substitute $x = 0.0100\text{ M}$ into the denominator: $(0.100 - 0.010)^2(0.050 - 0.010) = (0.090)^2(0.040) = (0.0081)(0.040) = 0.000324\text{ M}^3$. Evaluating the quotient: $\frac{0.0100}{0.000324} = \frac{1000}{32.4} \approx 30.864\text{ M}^{-2}$, which matches $K_{\text{ex}}$ exactly! Therefore, $x = 0.0100\text{ M} = 10.0\text{ mM}$. Step 4: The fraction of initial crown ether complexed is: $\%\,\text{complexed} = \frac{x}{[\text{DC18C6}]_0} \times 100\% = \frac{0.0100\text{ M}}{0.050\text{ M}} \times 100\% = 20.0\%$. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Anhydrous beryllium chloride exhibits distinctive coordination environments and electron counts across different physical aggregation states and coordination adducts:
(I) In solid crystalline polymeric beryllium chloride, $(\text{BeCl}_2)_n$, let $x$ be the formal coordination number of each beryllium center.
(II) In the volatile basic beryllium acetate complex, $\text{Be}_4\text{O}(\text{CH}_3\text{COO})_6$, let $y$ be the coordination number of the central oxygen atom.
(III) In gaseous monomeric beryllium chloride, $\text{BeCl}_2(g)$, present at temperatures above $1200\text{ K}$, let $z$ be the number of valence shell electrons surrounding the central beryllium atom.
Determine the integer value of $(10 \times x) + (5 \times y) + z$.
questions.explanation: Step 1: In solid $(\text{BeCl}_2)_n$, beryllium attains octet completion by forming an infinite linear polymer of edge-sharing tetrahedra where each chlorine atom acts as a bridging ligand. Each beryllium atom is bonded to 4 chlorine atoms ($sp^3$ hybridization). Therefore, coordination number $x = 4$. Step 2: In basic beryllium acetate, $\text{Be}_4\text{O}(\text{CH}_3\text{COO})_6$, a central oxygen atom is located at the center of a regular tetrahedron whose four vertices are occupied by four beryllium atoms. Thus, the central oxygen atom is bonded to 4 beryllium atoms ($sp^3$ hybridized central oxygen), giving coordination number $y = 4$. Step 3: In gaseous monomeric $\text{BeCl}_2(g)$ at $1200\text{ K}$, the molecule is linear ($sp$ hybridization, $\text{Cl-Be-Cl}$). Beryllium forms two single covalent bonds with chlorine and has no lone pairs, meaning it possesses only 4 valence electrons in its outer shell (an electron-deficient, hypovalent sextet/octet violation). Therefore, $z = 4$. Step 4: Substituting these values into the required arithmetic expression: $(10 \times x) + (5 \times y) + z = (10 \times 4) + (5 \times 4) + 4 = 40 + 20 + 4 = 64$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the vapor phase at $750\text{ K}$, monomeric beryllium chloride exists in dynamic dimerization equilibrium with its chloro-bridged planar dimer: $2\text{BeCl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Be}_2\text{Cl}_4(g)$. Thermodynamic analysis provides a standard enthalpy of dimerization $\Delta H^\circ = -105.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ and a standard entropy of dimerization $\Delta S^\circ = -120.0\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$. Assuming ideal gas behavior and that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ remain constant with temperature, calculate the equilibrium constant $K_p$ (in $\text{bar}^{-1}$) at $750\text{ K}$, and determine the equilibrium mole fraction of the dimer $\text{Be}_2\text{Cl}_4$ ($y_{\text{dimer}}$) in a vapor mixture maintained at a total pressure of $1.00\text{ bar}$. ($R = 8.314\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$).
options: A) $K_p \approx 11.1\text{ bar}^{-1}$ and $y_{\text{dimer}} \approx 0.741$
B) $K_p \approx 0.090\text{ bar}^{-1}$ and $y_{\text{dimer}} \approx 0.076$
C) $K_p \approx 11.1\text{ bar}^{-1}$ and $y_{\text{dimer}} \approx 0.259$
D) $K_p \approx 1.25\text{ bar}^{-1}$ and $y_{\text{dimer}} \approx 0.450$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compute the standard Gibbs energy of dimerization at $750\text{ K}$ using $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$: $\Delta G^\circ = -105000\text{ J/mol} - (750\text{ K})(-120.0\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}) = -105000 + 90000 = -15000\text{ J/mol} = -15.0\text{ kJ/mol}$. Step 2: The equilibrium constant $K_p$ is obtained from: $\ln K_p = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT} = -\frac{-15000\text{ J/mol}}{(8.314\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)})(750\text{ K})} = \frac{15000}{6235.5} \approx 2.4056$. Thus, $K_p = e^{2.4056} \approx 11.085\text{ bar}^{-1} \approx 11.1\text{ bar}^{-1}$. Step 3: Let $y$ be the mole fraction of $\text{Be}_2\text{Cl}_4(g)$ at equilibrium. The mole fraction of monomer $\text{BeCl}_2(g)$ is $(1 - y)$. Since total pressure $P = 1.00\text{ bar}$, the partial pressures are $P_{\text{dimer}} = y\text{ bar}$ and $P_{\text{monomer}} = (1 - y)\text{ bar}$. Step 4: Setting up the equilibrium relation: $K_p = \frac{P_{\text{dimer}}}{(P_{\text{monomer}})^2} = \frac{y}{(1 - y)^2} = 11.085$. Rearranging into a standard quadratic equation: $11.085(1 - 2y + y^2) = y \implies 11.085y^2 - 23.170y + 11.085 = 0$, or dividing by $11.085$: $y^2 - 2.0902y + 1.000 = 0$. Step 5: Solving for the physical root ($y < 1$): $y = \frac{2.0902 - \sqrt{(2.0902)^2 - 4(1)(1)}}{2} = \frac{2.0902 - \sqrt{4.3689 - 4}}{2} = \frac{2.0902 - 0.6074}{2} = \frac{1.4828}{2} \approx 0.7414 \approx 0.741$. Distractor C reports the monomer mole fraction ($1 - 0.741 = 0.259$). Option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Beryllium halides exhibit striking anomalous structural and bonding properties compared to the purely ionic halides of the heavier alkaline earth metals ($\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Sr}^{2+}, \text{Ba}^{2+}$). Which of the following statements regarding the structural chemistry and Lewis acidity of beryllium halides is/are CORRECT?
options: A) In the solid state, crystalline $(\text{BeCl}_2)_n$ forms an infinite polymeric chain of corner-sharing tetrahedra where each bridging chlorine donates an electron pair into a vacant $2p$ orbital of an adjacent Be atom, producing an internal $\text{Be-Cl-Be}$ bridging angle of approximately $82^\circ$

B) Beryllium fluoride ($\text{BeF}_2$) forms a 3D network structure isomorphous with $\beta\text{-quartz}$ consisting of corner-sharing $[\text{BeF}_4]$ tetrahedra, which on melting yields an extraordinarily viscous liquid with very low electrical conductivity due to retention of network covalent bonding

C) Because the gaseous monomer $\text{Cl-Be-Cl}$ has two vacant mutually orthogonal $2p$ atomic orbitals on the sp-hybridized beryllium atom, it acts as a strong Lewis acid, forming tetrahedral coordination complexes such as $[\text{BeCl}_2(\text{OEt}_2)_2]$ upon reaction with ethers

D) Unlike magnesium chloride solutions which are neutral ($pH \approx 7$), aqueous solutions of $\text{BeCl}_2$ are strongly acidic ($pH < 4$) due to pronounced cation hydrolysis of the tetrahedral aqua complex: $[\text{Be(H}_2\text{O)}_4]^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons [\text{Be(H}_2\text{O)}_3(\text{OH})]^+ + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Statement A is CORRECT: Solid $\text{BeCl}_2$ is a 1D coordination polymer where Be is $sp^3$ hybridized. The $\text{Be}_2\text{Cl}_2$ four-membered rings have an acute bridging angle $\angle\text{Be-Cl-Be} \approx 82^\circ$ and $\angle\text{Cl-Be-Cl} \approx 98^\circ$, reflecting high strain and dative bond character. Step 2: Statement B is CORRECT: $\text{BeF}_2$ is unique among Group 2 fluorides in adopting a quartz-like network of corner-sharing $[\text{BeF}_4]$ units. Upon melting at $552^\circ\text{C}$, the network does not break down into free mobile ions, producing a highly viscous melt with low ionic conductivity. Step 3: Statement C is CORRECT: Monomeric $\text{BeCl}_2$ has only four valence electrons; its two unoccupied $2p$ orbitals readily accept lone pairs from Lewis bases like diethyl ether to form stable, tetrahedral, four-coordinate adducts $[\text{BeCl}_2(\text{OEt}_2)_2]$. Step 4: Statement D is CORRECT: Small $\text{Be}^{2+}$ has a very high charge-to-radius ratio (polarizing power $\sim 64\text{ nm}^{-1}$), severely polarizing the O-H bonds of coordinated water molecules in $[\text{Be(H}_2\text{O)}_4]^{2+}$ ($pK_a \approx 5.4$), rendering aqueous solutions acidic. Statements A, B, C, and D are all correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: A high-grade Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) clinker contains $60.0\text{ mass }\%$ alite (tricalcium silicate, $\text{Ca}_3\text{SiO}_5$, $\text{C}_3\text{S}$, molar mass $228.3\text{ g/mol}$) and $10.0\text{ mass }\%$ tricalcium aluminate ($\text{Ca}_3\text{Al}_2\text{O}_6$, $\text{C}_3\text{A}$, molar mass $270.2\text{ g/mol}$). The complete stoichiometric hydration of alite proceeds according to: $2\text{Ca}_3\text{SiO}_5(s) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to 3\text{CaO}\cdot 2\text{SiO}_2\cdot 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) + 3\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)$, with a specific heat release of $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}} = 500.0\text{ J/g}$ of $\text{C}_3\text{S}$. The complete hydration of $\text{C}_3\text{A}$ to ettringite releases $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}} = 1160.0\text{ J/g}$ of $\text{C}_3\text{A}$. For a $1.000\text{ kg}$ batch of this dry cement undergoing complete hydration, calculate the total mass of crystalline calcium hydroxide ($\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, molar mass $74.1\text{ g/mol}$) liberated by alite hydration, and determine the combined total heat released (in $\text{kJ}$) from the hydration of both the $\text{C}_3\text{S}$ and $\text{C}_3\text{A}$ fractions.
options: A) $292.1\text{ g}$ of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and $416.0\text{ kJ}$ of heat
B) $194.7\text{ g}$ of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and $416.0\text{ kJ}$ of heat
C) $292.1\text{ g}$ of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and $832.0\text{ kJ}$ of heat
D) $584.2\text{ g}$ of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and $300.0\text{ kJ}$ of heat
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate the masses of $\text{C}_3\text{S}$ and $\text{C}_3\text{A}$ in $1.000\text{ kg} = 1000.0\text{ g}$ of cement clinker: $m(\text{C}_3\text{S}) = 0.600 \times 1000.0\text{ g} = 600.0\text{ g}$, and $m(\text{C}_3\text{A}) = 0.100 \times 1000.0\text{ g} = 100.0\text{ g}$. Step 2: Calculate moles of $\text{C}_3\text{S}$: $n(\text{C}_3\text{S}) = \frac{600.0\text{ g}}{228.3\text{ g/mol}} \approx 2.6281\text{ mol}$. From the balanced equation, $2\text{ moles of }\text{C}_3\text{S}$ produce $3\text{ moles of }\text{Ca(OH)}_2$. Therefore, moles of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ produced is: $n(\text{Ca(OH)}_2) = \frac{3}{2} \times 2.6281\text{ mol} = 3.9422\text{ mol}$. Step 3: Calculate the mass of liberated calcium hydroxide: $m(\text{Ca(OH)}_2) = 3.9422\text{ mol} \times 74.1\text{ g/mol} \approx 292.12\text{ g} \approx 292.1\text{ g}$. Distractor B arises from using a $1:1$ stoichiometric ratio ($194.7\text{ g}$). Step 4: Calculate the total heat released by hydration: From $\text{C}_3\text{S}$: $Q_1 = 600.0\text{ g} \times 500.0\text{ J/g} = 300000\text{ J} = 300.0\text{ kJ}$. From $\text{C}_3\text{A}$: $Q_2 = 100.0\text{ g} \times 1160.0\text{ J/g} = 116000\text{ J} = 116.0\text{ kJ}$. Combined heat released: $Q_{\text{total}} = Q_1 + Q_2 = 300.0 + 116.0 = 416.0\text{ kJ}$. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the manufacturing of Portland cement, tricalcium aluminate ($\text{Ca}_3\text{Al}_2\text{O}_6$, $\text{C}_3\text{A}$, molar mass $270.2\text{ g/mol}$) reacts violently with water, triggering premature flash setting. To retard this reaction, mineral gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, molar mass $172.2\text{ g/mol}$) is added during clinker grinding. Gypsum retards setting by reacting with $\text{C}_3\text{A}$ and water to form an insoluble barrier of ettringite on the aluminate grains: $\text{C}_3\text{A}(s) + 3(\text{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O})(s) + 26\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to \text{Ca}_6\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(\text{OH})_{12} \cdot 26\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)$ (ettringite). If an industrial clinker batch contains exactly $13.51\text{ kg}$ of pure $\text{C}_3\text{A}$, calculate the theoretical minimum number of moles of mineral gypsum required to completely convert all of the tricalcium aluminate into ettringite.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Convert the mass of tricalcium aluminate ($\text{C}_3\text{A}$) into grams: $m(\text{C}_3\text{A}) = 13.51\text{ kg} = 13510\text{ g}$. Step 2: Compute the number of moles of $\text{C}_3\text{A}$ present using its molar mass ($270.2\text{ g/mol}$): $n(\text{C}_3\text{A}) = \frac{13510\text{ g}}{270.2\text{ g/mol}} = 50.00\text{ mol}$. Step 3: From the balanced stoichiometric equation for ettringite synthesis: $1\text{ mol of }\text{C}_3\text{A}$ consumes exactly $3\text{ moles of mineral gypsum } (\text{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O})$. Step 4: Calculate the required moles of mineral gypsum: $n(\text{gypsum}) = 3 \times n(\text{C}_3\text{A}) = 3 \times 50.00\text{ mol} = 150\text{ mol}$. The resulting integer answer is therefore 150.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Isothermal conduction calorimetry during Portland cement hydration reveals a characteristic rate of heat evolution curve ($dQ/dt$ vs time) characterized by five distinct kinetic stages: Stage I (initial rapid exothermic pre-induction dissolution, $0\text{--}15\text{ min}$), Stage II (dormant or induction period, $15\text{ min to } 3\text{ h}$), Stage III (acceleration period, $3\text{ to } 12\text{ h}$), Stage IV (deceleration period), and Stage V (slow steady-state diffusion). Which of the following mechanistic models correctly explains the molecular origin of the Dormant Period (Stage II) and the subsequent onset of the Acceleration Period (Stage III)?
options: A) During Stage I, rapid superficial dissolution creates a thin, passivating metastable barrier layer of amorphous C-S-H and electric double-layer charges on $\text{C}_3\text{S}$ grains; Stage II persists while pore solution calcium and silicate concentrations reach critical supersaturation; Stage III initiates when stable crystalline C-S-H and $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ nucleate and rupture the barrier layer
B) Stage II is caused by endothermic evaporation of water from the pore channels, which absorbs heat and prevents chemical reaction until all water has evaporated
C) Stage II occurs because gypsum completely consumes all available calcium ions, preventing alite from dissolving until Stage III
D) Stage II is a thermodynamic dead-state where the Gibbs free energy change of hydration $\Delta G$ temporarily becomes positive, only returning to negative values in Stage III
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the initial minutes of hydration (Stage I), alite ($	ext{C}_3	ext{S}$) undergoes rapid incongruent surface dissolution, releasing $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, $\text{OH}^-$, and silicate ions into the pore solution. Step 2: The dormant period (Stage II) is governed by two complementary phenomena: the rapid formation of an initial protective, semi-permeable, metastable barrier layer of amorphous C-S-H on the $\text{C}_3\text{S}$ grain surfaces, combined with a classical nucleation barrier. During this period, the rate of dissolution drops by orders of magnitude while the pore solution progressively accumulates $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ ions to reach a high degree of supersaturation with respect to portlandite ($\text{Ca(OH)}_2$) and stable C-S-H gel. Step 3: Stage III (acceleration) begins as soon as critical supersaturation triggers explosive heterogeneous nucleation and rapid growth of stable fibrillar C-S-H and macroscopic $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ crystals. This crystal growth bursts and exfoliates the initial protective surface barrier, providing fresh unhydrated $\text{C}_3\text{S}$ surfaces to water and unleashing rapid heat liberation. Hence, option A is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Basic beryllium acetate, with molecular formula $[\text{Be}_4\text{O}(\text{CH}_3\text{COO})_6]$, is synthesized by dissolving beryllium carbonate in glacial acetic acid. Which of the following statements regarding the molecular geometry, electronic bonding, and chemical behavior of basic beryllium acetate is/are CORRECT?
options: A) The molecule features a central oxygen atom located at the center of a regular tetrahedron whose four vertices are occupied by four beryllium atoms, with the central oxygen being formally $sp^3$ hybridized
B) The six acetate groups act as bidentate bridging carboxylate ligands, each spanning one of the six edges of the central $\text{Be}_4$ tetrahedron through two oxygen atoms
C) Each beryllium atom achieves a coordination number of 4 and an approximately tetrahedral $sp^3$ coordination geometry, bonded to the central oxygen and three carboxylate oxygens

D) Basic beryllium acetate is a discrete, covalent, non-electrolyte molecule that dissolves readily in non-polar organic solvents such as benzene and chloroform, and sublimes undecomposed at $330^\circ\text{C}$ at atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Step 1: Statement A is CORRECT: In $[\text{Be}_4\text{O}(\text{CH}_3\text{COO})_6]$, single-crystal X-ray crystallography establishes a tetrahedral core of four Be atoms surrounding an interstitial central oxygen atom ($mu_4\text{-O}$). The central oxygen forms four equivalent $\text{O-Be}$ covalent/dative bonds pointing towards the vertices of a regular tetrahedron ($T_d$ molecular symmetry). Step 2: Statement B is CORRECT: A regular tetrahedron possesses 6 edges. Each of the six acetate ligands bridges one edge between two Be atoms via a $\text{Be-O-C(CH}_3\text{)-O-Be}$ chelate-like bridge. Step 3: Statement C is CORRECT: Each Be atom is bonded to 1 central $\mu_4$-oxygen and 3 separate acetate oxygens, giving Be a coordination number of 4 and fulfilling the octet rule ($sp^3$ hybridization). Step 4: Statement D is CORRECT: The non-polar peripheral methyl groups completely encase the polar $\text{Be}_4\text{O}$ core in an organic lipophilic shell. Consequently, it exhibits covalent properties, high solubility in nonpolar solvents (benzene, $\text{CHCl}_3$), and readily sublimes ($330^\circ\text{C}$) without decomposition. All four statements A, B, C, and D are correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
In cement manufacturing chemistry, the Lime Saturation Factor (LSF) controls the equilibrium phase ratio between alite ($\text{C}_3\text{S}$, early strength phase) and belite ($\text{C}_2\text{S}$, late strength phase) and prevents the presence of deleterious uncombined free lime. The Lime Saturation Factor is defined by the standard formula:
$$\text{LSF} = \frac{\%\text{CaO} - 0.7(\%\text{SO}_3)}{2.8(\%\text{SiO}_2) + 1.2(\%\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3) + 0.65(\%\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3)}$$
where oxide compositions are expressed in mass percentages. An industrial rotary kiln clinker with negligible sulfur content ($\%\text{SO}_3 = 0.00\%$) yields the following mass oxide composition:
$$\%\text{CaO} = 64.75\%,\quad \%\text{SiO}_2 = 21.00\%,\quad \%\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 5.00\%,\quad \%\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 = 3.00\%$$
Calculate the value of the Lime Saturation Factor multiplied by $100$ ($100 \times \text{LSF}$), rounded to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Evaluate the numerator of the LSF equation: $\text{Numerator} = \%\text{CaO} - 0.7(\%\text{SO}_3) = 64.75 - 0.7(0.00) = 64.75$. Step 2: Evaluate the denominator term by term using the oxide mass percentages: Term 1: $2.8 \times \%\text{SiO}_2 = 2.8 \times 21.00 = 58.80$. Term 2: $1.2 \times \%\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 1.2 \times 5.00 = 6.00$. Term 3: $0.65 \times \%\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 = 0.65 \times 3.00 = 1.95$. Step 3: Sum the denominator terms: $\text{Denominator} = 58.80 + 6.00 + 1.95 = 66.75$. Step 4: Calculate the Lime Saturation Factor: $\text{LSF} = \frac{64.75}{66.75} = \frac{259}{267} \approx 0.970037$. Step 5: Multiplying by 100 yields: $100 \times \text{LSF} = 97.0037$. Rounding to the nearest integer gives 97.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In a competitive biphasic extraction experiment at $298\text{ K}$, an aqueous solution containing an equimolar mixture of $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{K}^+$ cations ($0.020\text{ M}$ each) and excess lipophilic picrate ($\text{Pic}^-$) is equilibrated with an equal volume of chloroform containing [2.2.1]-cryptand. The macrobicyclic cavity diameter of [2.2.1]-cryptand is $2.2\text{ \AA}$, and its stability constants for alkali metal encapsulation are $K_f(\text{Na}^+) = 1.00 \times 10^5\text{ M}^{-1}$ and $K_f(\text{K}^+) = 2.50 \times 10^3\text{ M}^{-1}$. Calculate the competitive selectivity separation factor $\beta = \frac{[\text{Na}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}} \cdot [\text{K}^+]_{\text{aq}}}{[\text{K}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}} \cdot [\text{Na}^+]_{\text{aq}}}$, and determine the relative percentage purity of $\text{Na}^+$ among the extracted alkali metal cryptate complexes in the organic chloroform phase.
options: A) $\beta = 40.0$; $\text{Na}^+$ is extracted with $97.6\%$ relative purity into the organic phase
B) $\beta = 25.0$; $\text{K}^+$ is extracted with $96.2\%$ relative purity into the organic phase
C) $\beta = 40.0$; $\text{K}^+$ is extracted with $97.6\%$ relative purity into the organic phase
D) $\beta = 0.025$; $\text{Na}^+$ is extracted with $2.4\%$ relative purity into the organic phase
questions.explanation: Step 1: The competitive extraction equilibrium is governed by the cation exchange between cryptate complexes: $\text{Na}^+(aq) + [\text{K}(\text{crypt})]^+(org) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Na}(\text{crypt})]^+(org) + \text{K}^+(aq)$. Step 2: The selectivity separation factor $\beta$ is given by the ratio of individual cryptate formation constants: $\beta = \frac{[\text{Na}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}} \cdot [\text{K}^+]_{\text{aq}}}{[\text{K}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}} \cdot [\text{Na}^+]_{\text{aq}}} = \frac{K_f(\text{Na}^+)}{K_f(\text{K}^+)} = \frac{1.00 \times 10^5\text{ M}^{-1}}{2.50 \times 10^3\text{ M}^{-1}} = 40.0$. Step 3: In an equimolar initial aqueous mixture where $[\text{Na}^+]_{\text{aq}} \approx [\text{K}^+]_{\text{aq}}$, the ratio of complexed cations in the organic phase is: $\frac{[\text{Na}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}}}{[\text{K}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}}} = \beta = 40.0$. Step 4: The relative percentage purity of sodium in the extracted organic phase is: $\%\,\text{Na} = \frac{[\text{Na}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}}}{[\text{Na}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}} + [\text{K}(\text{crypt})^+]_{\text{org}}} \times 100\% = \frac{40.0}{40.0 + 1.0} \times 100\% = \frac{40.0}{41.0} \times 100\% \approx 97.56\% \approx 97.6\%$. Step 5: The cavity of [2.2.1]-cryptand ($2.2\text{ \AA}$) matches the ionic diameter of $\text{Na}^+$ ($2.04\text{ \AA}$) far better than the larger $\text{K}^+$ ($2.76\text{ \AA}$), explaining why sodium is preferentially extracted. Option A is correct.
